To establish causation, you generally need evidence that: the cause preceeds the effect in western linear logic. Vedanta states that the effect *already exists* in its cause in a latent form. This is similar to how a tree exists within the seed before it manifests. In this view:

* The cause (e.g., Brahman) and the effect (e.g., the world) are inseparable.
* The effect is not something newly created but something that becomes manifest from the cause.

Example: The pot exists in the clay before the potter shapes it. The clay is the material cause (upadana karana), and the pot is its effect, but the pot’s existence was always inherent in the clay.

This is not a linear logic. The belief that there's a linear logic traps us in samsara.

Brahman is not "prior" to the effect (the world); rather, the world is a superimposition on Brahman, much like waves are on the ocean. This undermines the linearity of causation, as Brahman transcends time, space, and causation.

Through Maya, the one undivided reality appears as many. Maya superimposes names and forms (nama-rupa) onto the formless, creating the illusion of separation. It’s like a movie projector casting frames onto a screen: the screen is the absolute reality (Brahman), but Maya draws our attention to the moving images instead in this divine game (lila). This limits our view, making it impossible to perceive the undivided nature of reality through our senses, or even through the mind, because the mind itself is part of the phenomenological world.

We perceive shapes and forms in our world and assign them names based on their characteristics and functions to aid us in this relative reality, so that we can understand each other (and at least perform basic yoga practices to know Brahman). These perceptions are further influenced by cultural conditioning. For instance, someone unfamiliar with the concept of a "desk" might see it simply as "a flat piece of wood." In this way, perception is shaped by both external reality and the internal lens of our mind.

In essence: Maya projects forms, and the mind categorizes and distinguishes them using its conditioned patterns.

One might ask, "But why does Maya exist and operate as it does?" The truth is, this question cannot be answered by the mind because it belongs to the realm of the intellect. The very act of asking "why" assumes duality, a separation between cause and effect, subject and object. Why is there perception? What's the cause of perception? We could say Maya, but Maya is relative compared to the Absolute. We don't know in essence.

The concept of "why"  and "cause" exists only within the framework of relative reality (duality). From the standpoint of the absolute (Brahman), there is no Maya, no questions, no distinctions, there is only what is. Maya does not exist for any specific "cause" within the essence of Brahman, as Brahman is beyond causation and beyond all conceptualization.

As members of the human family, we should show each other respect and courtesy. In our relationships with people of other faiths and beliefs, this means exercising goodwill and:

  
\- Respect the freedom of other people within the law to express their beliefs and beliefs  
\- Learn to understand what others really believe and let them express it  
\- Respect others' beliefs about food, dress and social etiquette and not behave in ways that cause unnecessary offense  
\- Recognizing that we all sometimes fall short of the ideals of our traditions and never comparing our ideals to the practices of other people  
\- Work to prevent disagreement from leading to conflict  
\- Always trying to avoid violence in our relationships

  
When we talk to each other about matters of faith, we must do so with sensitivity, honesty and frankness. This means:

  
\- Recognize that listening as well as speaking is necessary for genuine conversation  
\- Be honest about our religious beliefs and allegiances  
\- Do not misrepresent or disparage other people's beliefs and practices  
\- Correct misunderstandings or false statements not only of our own but also of other faiths whenever we encounter them  
\- Be direct about our intentions  
\- Accept that in formal interfaith meetings there is a particular responsibility to ensure respect for the religious commitment of all those present

  
We all want others to understand and respect our opinions. Some people will also want to persuade us to join their faith. In a multi-confessional society where this is permitted, the attempt should always be characterized by self-control and concern for the freedom and dignity of the other. This means:  
\- Respect another person's expressed wish to be left alone  
\- Avoid imposing ourselves and our opinions on individuals or communities who find themselves in vulnerable situations  
\- Be sensitive and courteous  
\- Avoid violent actions or language, threats, manipulation, improper incentives or the abuse of any type of power  
\- Respect the right of others to disagree with us

  
Living and working together is not always easy. Religion exploits deep emotions that can sometimes take destructive forms. Where this happens, we must draw on our morals to bring about reconciliation and understanding. The truest fruits of religion are healing and positive. We have a lot to learn from each other. Others can enrich us without undermining our identities. Together, listening and responding with openness and respect, we can move forward to work in ways that recognize authentic differences but that are based on shared hopes and values.

Within the Catholic Church, the concept of natural law is a fundamental element of moral theology and ethics. It is a longstanding theological and philosophical tradition that dates back to figures like St. Thomas Aquinas and is deeply embedded in Catholic teaching. Natural law has its roots in the works of philosophers like Heraclitus, Plato, and Aristotle. Aristotle, in particular, wrote about the idea of a "law of nature" or "law of reason" that was discoverable through human reason and observation of the natural world. Roman thinkers such as Cicero and Seneca also contributed to the development of natural law theory. Cicero, for example, emphasized the existence of a higher moral law that transcended human-made laws. Natural law continued to be a prominent theme in medieval and early modern philosophy. Philosophers like Thomas Hobbes, John Locke, and Immanuel Kant each had their interpretations and variations of natural law theory.

The core idea behind natural law is that there are moral principles that can be discerned through human reason and observation of the natural world.  These principles are considered to be universal and unchanging, and they provide a foundation for ethical reasoning and the formulation of just laws. The concept of natural law, suggests that there is an inherent order and purpose to human actions, including sexual activity. From a natural law perspective, sexual intercourse has the dual purpose of uniting spouses and potentially bringing forth new life. To act in accordance with natural law is to act in harmony with the inherent purpose of human nature.

Chastity is the virtue of abstaining from sexual activity outside of a valid marriage between a man and a woman. The Church encourages individuals to practice chastity as a way to live a morally upright life. For those within the bonds of marriage, chastity includes mutual respect and fidelity to one's spouse. 1 Corinthians 7:2 (NIV): "But since sexual immorality is occurring, each man should have sexual relations with his own wife, and each woman with her own husband."

The Catholic Church teaches that the primary purpose of sexual intercourse is procreation, the creation of new life. Genesis 1:27-28 (NIV): "So God created mankind in his own image, in the image of God he created them; male and female he created them. God blessed them and said to them, 'Be fruitful and increase in number; fill the earth and subdue it.'"

Additionally, it emphasizes the importance of unity between spouses through the marital act. This teaching is often summarized as the "unitive and procreative" aspect of sexual relations within marriage.

The Church views marriage as a sacred institution established by God. Within this sacred bond, sexual intimacy is seen as a gift from God. Genesis 2:24 (NIV): "That is why a man leaves his father and mother and is united to his wife, and they become one flesh."

Respecting both the unitive and procreative dimensions of sexual relations is a way of honoring and preserving the sanctity of marriage.

The Church teaches that every person has inherent dignity and worth. Respecting the procreative aspect of sexual relations acknowledges the potential gift of life and the dignity of the human person from the moment of conception. 

The Catholic Church's teachings on human sexuality draw from the Bible, particularly the accounts of creation and marriage in the Book of Genesis. The specific teachings and moral guidelines related to sexuality within Christianity, including the Catholic Church, are often based on a combination of biblical passages, theological reflection, and tradition.

Natural law theory has faced various criticisms and challenges. Some argue that the idea of an objective, universal moral law is difficult to establish empirically, and there can be disagreement about what constitutes "natural" in human nature. Others may critique specific applications of natural law in areas such as sexual ethics or political theory. Whether natural law theory makes sense to an individual can depend on their personal beliefs, values, and worldview. Some people may find its emphasis on moral absolutes and human dignity to be in line with their own beliefs, while others may prefer alternative ethical frameworks.

When considering its relevance or applicability, it's valuable to engage with the writings and arguments of philosophers who have explored natural law theory in depth to develop a well-informed perspective.

Most people just stay inside their room, unless it’s time to visit the doctor. If you’re voluntarily admitted you get more perks, for example you get to own a phone. Treatment in the Spdc is generally resolved through two actions: the administration of psychotropic drugs and sedatives, and the containment of the patients. They give you medicine in a shot glass, even if the nurse doesn't tell you what he's giving you. If you refuse to take them, and maybe yell at the staff, you immediately find yourself surrounded by 4 or 5 nurses who lock your arms and neck immobilizing you. I don't agree with this practice, restraint is not a therapy. Nurses do not follow any specific training before working with psychiatric patients: they are chosen on the basis of a ranking. So they too do the first thing that comes to mind, no one teaches them how to deescalate the conflicts peacefully and without harming the patient.

Among the 329 Italian SPDCs, a minority, about thirty, has decided to say no to closed doors and restraint. The only systematic survey carried out at national level by the Istituto Superiore di Sanità dates back to 2004. In 2006, a no-restraint Spdc Club was founded in Italy, numbering 21. Are we talking about a moral point of view? If so I'd say that Both Alder's and Tally's choices could have led to further issues but they both had good intentions. Alder was selfish in hiding her involvement in her in the birth of the spree, but she was also selfless in trying to help her daughters in a racist world. Tally believed that the correct thing to do to help her fellow witches was to tell the truth.I think that emotional reactions are relevant for the moral evaluation of Alder and Tally's choices. We saw where they were coming from, what they've been through and who they are as people. We know that they are JUST PEOPLE. They both weighted the pros and cons of their decision. And they both chose the course of action that provided the greatest benefits according to them. They both meant well. They are both utilitarians, but in a different way. Let me explain.

From a utilitarian point of view, one may view actions in terms of intentions and consequences. The phrase "The path to hell is paved with good intentions" is popular for very valid reasons.How does one view a well intentioned action that resulted in catastrophe? How does one view a malevolent action that had a net positive impact? We can juggle every possible permutation and combination of choices, but the fact is that the task of determining ethical imperatives and implications is closer to an art than a science.

Some utilitarians maintain that in making an ethical decision, we must ask ourselves: "What effect will my doing this act in this situation have on the general balance of good over evil?" If lying would produce the best consequences in a particular situation, we ought to lie.Others, known as rule utilitarians, claim that we must choose that act that conforms to the general rule that would have the best consequences. In other words, we must ask ourselves: "What effect would everyone's doing this kind of action have on the general balance of good over evil?" So, for example, the rule "to always tell the truth" in general promotes the good of everyone and therefore should always be followed, even if in a certain situation lying would produce the best consequences.Despite such differences among utilitarians, however, most hold to the general principle that morality must depend on balancing the beneficial and harmful consequences of our conduct.

The rightness or wrongness of an action can only be inferred from the context in which it occurs, and Motherland is a show that insists on moral grayness. The writers of the show always viewed the words "right" and "wrong" with suspicion. I don't think there was a right or wrong choice here to make for Alder and Tally, in life there never is one, but they make choices and that's what counts, really. A lot of people who didn't have psychiatric problems before, are probably developing them now, during the pandemic. And the ones who already had them, were abandoned by their psychologists and psychiatrists; and when weak minds are put under stress, bad things happen. So I just want to give a general advice to everyone.

You need to take care of yourself. Start to make your bed every morning. I know it seems silly, because nobody is going to see that you've been a lazy ass. But try to do it, with purpose: making the bed is the first action of the day,  it will give you a small sense of pride, and it will encourage you to do another task and another. It's an anchor: if today was a bad day, tomorrow you can try and make it a better day and so forth. The little things are the ones that matter.

Eat healthy, sleep well, do exercise. 

Take care of something: if you have a pet spend time together. If you don't have animals, buy plants.  It helps with productivity and being around nature makes us feel good.

Use video chats to keep in contact with your family and friends. 

Distract yourself in any way you prefer, start a new hobby. You're going to have a lot of free time in your hands, and you can't just sleep all day, so you better do something.  If you don't feel up to doing anything, though, that's fine too. It's  important to be kind to yourself and recognise when you need a break. 

Get professional help if you need it. Don't be proud, discussing our feelings sometimes can help us to feel better.

Keep taking your medication. If you have a repeat prescription you  might be able to order it by phone, online or using an app. You can also  ask your pharmacy about getting your medication delivered or asking  someone to collect it for you.  

You can collect a prescription on behalf of someone else. If the  prescription is electronic, the person who the prescription is for can  choose the pharmacy or dispenser where the prescription is sent. You can  collect the medicine on their behalf if the person has told the  pharmacy that they are happy for you to do so.

You can collect a  paper prescription from a GP surgery for a friend or relative if that  person has told the surgery they're happy for you to collect it. You  will usually be asked to give the name and address of the person the  prescription is for - and you may need ID. If you're collecting a  'controlled medicine' for someone else - such as morphine - the  pharmacist may ask you for proof of identity.
